head:
Health · Mind

Sport and mental health: what physical activity changes in the mind

Everyone has heard that exercise “does you good mentally”. This article checks what the studies actually allow us to say: for which difficulties, how strongly, at what dose, and where the evidence stops. The subject also touches on suicide, which is handled with care. If you are going through a difficult time, the helpline numbers are in the box further down.

Part 1 · The question

A phrase repeated everywhere, rarely checked

“Go for a run, it'll clear your head.” You have heard it, and perhaps said it. It actually contains three different promises. The first: moving makes you less sad or less anxious. The second: moving works like a treatment. The third, the heaviest, rarely spelled out but often implied: moving protects against the darkest thoughts.

These three promises do not rest on the same level of evidence. Some rely on trials in which people are randomly assigned to move or not to move. Others rely on simple observations: people who exercise feel better, but we do not know whether exercise helps them or whether feeling well makes them more likely to exercise. And for one of them, the answer is much thinner than people say.

This distinction concerns you directly. If you are counting on exercise to feel better, you want to know what you can expect from it and when it is no longer enough. If you train a lot, you want to know whether it still protects you. If you are worried about someone, you want to avoid promising them what science does not promise.

The question

When mental health wavers, what can we really expect from physical activity, at what dose and in what form, and where does the evidence stop, in particular for suicide?

We start from the widest view (hundreds of thousands of people observed), then narrow down: randomised trials, comparison with treatments, dose and type of activity, mechanisms, and finally the borderline cases: suicide, elite sport and excessive training.

Part 2 · What is at stake

What is at stake

Mental health is not a subject for specialists only. According to the WHO, nearly one billion people were living with a mental disorder worldwide in 2019, about one in eight. Depression and anxiety rose by a further 25% or more during the first year of the pandemic.5

In France, Santé publique France surveyed 24,514 adults by telephone in 2021 using a standardised WHO questionnaire. Result: 12.5% of 18-85 year-olds had experienced a major depressive episode in the previous twelve months.4 To see whether this share is growing, we compare with 2017 for the same age range.

The share of adults who experienced a depressive episode rose sharply in four years

Major depressive episode over 12 months, WHO CIDI-SF questionnaire, telephone surveys. Source: Santé publique France, Baromètre santé 2021 (BEH 2023, no. 2).4

What this means

In 2021, more than one young adult in five (20.8%) reported a depressive episode within the year, compared with 11.7% four years earlier: the largest increase of any age group. The authors also note a higher risk among women, people living alone, unemployed people and people in financial difficulty.4

Suicide, order of magnitude

According to the WHO, about 727,000 people died by suicide worldwide in 2021. About 73% of these deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries, and suicide was the third leading cause of death among 15-29 year-olds.1 In France, Santé publique France counts 8,848 deaths by suicide in 2023, a rate of 13 per 100,000 inhabitants. Nearly three deaths in four concern men, with the highest rates among men aged 65 and over (37 per 100,000) and aged 45 to 64 (29 per 100,000).2

Attempts cannot be read from the same figures. In 2024, hospitals treated 97,302 cases of self-harm, with particularly high rates among young women aged 11 to 17 and 18 to 24.2,3 The 3114, the national suicide prevention number, received 215,093 calls between June and December 2024.3

A suicide never has a single cause. The WHO lists among the risk factors mental disorders (especially depression and alcohol use), a previous attempt, and sudden events such as financial difficulties, a break-up, a painful illness, a bereavement, violence or isolation.1 Santé publique France adds that suicidal behaviours are strongly linked to the risk of depression.2

What this means

Depression affects a great many people and is one of the main risk factors for suicide. If exercise acts on one, it could weigh on the other, but that remains to be shown, not assumed. And promising a protection that no one has measured risks leaving someone alone with a suffering that needed a professional.

Part 3 · The demonstration
1The large-scale picture
rest:
Those who move feel better: this is observed in more than a million people

First level of evidence, the widest: comparing active and inactive people. In 2018, a team from Yale and Oxford used American surveys of 1.2 million adults. People who exercised reported 2.0 days of poor mental health per month, compared with 3.4 among those who did not, which is 43% fewer difficult days according to the study. Among people already diagnosed with depression, the gap was 7.1 versus 10.9 days.7

This figure says that, at comparable age, sex, income, weight and physical health, active people have fewer “difficult” days. It does not say why: it is a snapshot, based on self-reported answers.7

We can gain precision by looking at quantity. A meta-analysis of 15 studies that followed 191,130 adults over time finds that the risk of depression falls as the level of activity rises, and that the gain starts at a modest dose.8

Even half a dose of activity goes with less depression

Heights calculated from the published relative risks (0.82 and 0.75), and therefore derived. Activity reported by participants, not measured. Source: Pearce et al., JAMA Psychiatry, 2022.8

What this means

You do not need to train like an athlete: half the recommended dose goes with a risk about 18% lower, the minimum dose with about 25% less. As an order of magnitude, half a dose corresponds to about 75 minutes of moderate effort per week (a rough calculation: the recommendation is at least 150 minutes).8,31 This curve describes an association, not yet a cause.

The immediate objection: the arrow can point the other way

When you are depressed, you have neither the energy nor the desire to move. Depressed people therefore exercise less, and the graphs could be read backwards: it would not be exercise that protects, it would be depression that immobilises. The authors of the dose study acknowledge this.8

To sort this out, a 2019 study used genetic variations, present from birth and therefore independent of lifestyle (Mendelian randomisation). When activity was measured by a sensor, it went with less depression, and the reverse effect was not demonstrated. However, nothing appeared when activity was only self-reported.9 This is a clue in favour of a real effect, not definitive proof.

What this means

Large-scale observation establishes a strong and consistent link. It does not settle the question “does exercise make you feel better?”. For that, you have to randomly assign who moves and who does not. That is the next step.

2When people are randomly assigned

Randomised trials: the effect exists, it is moderate, and its size is still debated

A randomised trial answers the previous objection: people with depression are randomly divided between a group that trains and a control group. If the first group feels better, it is no longer because people in good shape are naturally more cheerful.

In 2023, an umbrella review published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine gathered 97 reviews, 1,039 trials and more than 128,000 participants. In adults with depression, physical activity reduces symptoms to a moderate degree compared with usual care, with an index of around 0.4 to 0.5 (0.43 for depression and 0.42 for anxiety, as median values). This index is a standardised difference: below 0.2 the effect is small, around 0.5 it is moderate, above 0.8 it is large.10

For depression, the Cochrane review, the reference for reviews on treatments, finds a moderate effect of 0.62 across all trials comparing exercise with no treatment. But it also sorts the trials by robustness. When only the six most rigorous trials are kept (allocation concealed from assessors, blinded assessment, analysis of all participants), the effect falls to 0.18, and is no longer statistically distinguishable from zero.11

The effect is clear across all trials, but becomes uncertain with the most rigorous trials

Figures read from the page of the 2026 update of the Cochrane review (Clegg et al.). The values are negative in the source (negative = fewer symptoms): they are reversed here so that the right-hand side means “exercise helps”. 95% intervals rounded, as published.11

What this means

The red line touches the zero line: with only the trials using the strongest methods, we cannot say that the effect exists, but we cannot say that it does not exist either (the interval runs from -0.11 to +0.47). This is not proof that exercise does not work. It is proof that the trials are still too small and too uneven to settle on a figure. The average effect of 0.62 may be overestimated, because weak trials tend to inflate results.11 After the programmes end, a smaller effect, of about 0.33, persists in the trials that followed participants.

Two types of exercise have been tested separately. For strength training, a meta-analysis of 33 trials (1,877 participants) finds a moderate effect of 0.66 on depressive symptoms, whatever the training volume.12

It remains to be seen whether it holds its own against usual treatments.

3Against treatments, then anxiety

Compared with a medication or a therapy, and for other forms of suffering than depression

The SMILE trial compared, in 156 adults aged 50 and over with major depression, 16 weeks of group aerobic exercise, an antidepressant (sertraline) or both. At the end, the three groups had improved to a comparable degree, with the medication acting faster at the start.14 Ten months later, the “exercise” group had relapsed less than the “medication” group.15 Reservations: no placebo group, group sessions (the social bond may have mattered as much as the effort), and 32 of the 156 people did not complete the protocol.14,35

Against therapy and medication, exercise is not distinguishable, but the trials are small

Standardised differences as published in the 2026 Cochrane update: -0.03 (from -0.32 to 0.26) for psychotherapy, -0.11 (from -0.34 to 0.12) for antidepressants, negative = exercise better. Signs reversed here for readability (derived).11

What this means

In both cases, the dot is close to zero and the line widely overlaps the zero line: we cannot say that exercise does worse, nor that it does better. Cochrane speaks of “probably little or no difference” with psychotherapy and “may be little or no difference” with medication, based on a very small number of trials.11 This is an argument for including movement in a care plan, not for stopping a treatment: none of these trials tests that.

Anxiety and stress

For anxiety disorders, the evidence is thinner. In adults without a diagnosed disorder, a meta-analysis of trials concludes that anxiety is reduced, with a small effect.16 In people who have an anxiety or stress-related disorder, another meta-analysis finds a moderate effect, but from only six trials.17 The 2023 umbrella review gives 0.42 for anxiety, of the same order as for depression, but with the same reservation about quality.10

What this means

Moving probably helps release pressure when you are tense or anxious, with a small to moderate effect. But it is less solid than for depression: few trials, of small size. If anxiety overwhelms you or holds you back, seeing a professional remains the first step.

It remains to be seen how much, and what.

4Dose and type

How much and in what form: what the data allow us to say, and not to say

For dose, we have already seen the result of the Pearce study: a benefit from half the recommended dose.8 The American study of 1.2 million people allows us to go further, by comparing types of activity and frequency. Note: it is cross-sectional, with self-reported answers, so it shows associations, not effects.7

All activities go with fewer difficult days, some more than others

Reductions adjusted for age, sex, income, education, employment, BMI and physical health. Self-reported activity. Source: Chekroud et al., The Lancet Psychiatry, 2018, via the ScienceDaily report.7

What this means

Of the 75 activities recorded, all are associated with an improvement, including household chores (about 10%). Team sports, cycling and aerobic exercise or the gym come in at around 20 to 22%. The differences between these three are too small to name a winner.

For frequency, the same study associates the best mental state with three to five sessions per week, and with sessions of 30 to 60 minutes. It also finds an opposite signal: exercising more than 23 times a month, or for more than 90 minutes per session, goes with a poorer mental state, and beyond three hours a day, poorer than not exercising at all. The authors suggest that this may reflect obsessive traits, an untested hypothesis.7 Because the study is cross-sectional, we do not know whether excess harms mood or whether a fragile mood pushes people to excess.

Trials shed a different light on type. In the network meta-analysis of 218 trials, walking or jogging (difference of 0.62), yoga (0.55), strength training (0.49), mixed aerobic exercise (0.43) and tai chi or qigong (0.42) all reduced depression symptoms compared with an active control group. The authors also write that the effect was proportional to the prescribed intensity, but give no figures. Strength training and yoga appeared to be the best accepted. Certainty is low for walking and jogging, very low for the others, and only one trial had a low risk of bias in the Cochrane sense.13

What this means

The figures by type of exercise do not allow a ranking, because their intervals overlap and certainty is low. What emerges from these sources: an effect for all the forms tested, a useful modest dose, a warning signal towards excess. The advice “do what you can keep up over time, without pushing yourself to the extreme” is the one that these data support best.

If the effect is real, how does it work?

5The mechanisms

Why it might work: three leads, one better documented

The honest answer: we do not yet know exactly. One review on the subject writes that the antidepressant mechanisms of physical activity “remain to be established”.18

The brain

Effort could act on the brain's plasticity (its ability to remodel itself), on inflammation and on stress hormones. A review of 100 articles published over twenty years on BDNF, a protein involved in this plasticity, reports that acute exercise, particularly intense exercise, increases it in healthy people as well as in patients. But in short-term studies, the change in blood BDNF was not linked to the severity of depression, and nothing shows that this rise causes the improvement in symptoms.19

Social bond and self-image

Training in a group breaks isolation, a risk factor for suicide cited by the WHO.1 Sticking to a programme and seeing your progress may strengthen the feeling of being able to act. These mechanisms are plausible, but the SMILE trial, for example, does not allow the effect of the effort to be separated from that of the group.14

Sleep

This is the most concrete lead. In France, 33.1% of adults aged 18 to 79 reported an insomnia complaint in 2024, and 21.5% were short sleepers, who have a higher risk of depression.6 Poor sleep is not only a symptom. A meta-analysis of 21 longitudinal studies indicates that people without depression who suffer from insomnia have about twice the risk of developing it (ratio of 2.1 in the fixed-effects model, 2.6 in the other).22

Now, exercise improves sleep, at least as people perceive it. A meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (1,806 adults) finds an improvement in sleep quality measured by questionnaire (-2.19 points on the PSQI scale), in insomnia (-1.52 on the ISI) and in daytime sleepiness (-2.55). Objective measures from wristbands show almost nothing, apart from better sleep efficiency. The risk of bias is high in all the trials (blinding is not possible).20 Another meta-analysis (9 trials, 557 participants) finds -2.87 PSQI points, but the effect is no longer significant without the weak trials.21

What this means

The link “move, sleep better, lower risk of depression” rests on three real findings: exercise improves perceived sleep, insomnia often precedes depression, and lack of sleep goes with more depression. But none of the sources read shows that sleep explains the effect of exercise on mood. It is a reasonable hypothesis, not a proven mechanism. In practice, you can monitor your sleep as a signal: if it deteriorates despite training, that is useful information.

It remains to test this picture against the two cases where it is most fragile: suicide, and elite sport.

6The borderline cases

Suicide, then elite sport: where the evidence thins out

What the studies on suicide actually show

This is the most delicate question, and therefore the one that calls for the most rigour. The best data come from Sweden: more than a million men who took the military service fitness test at age 18, with no known psychiatric illness, were followed for between 5 and 42 years.23

Low fitness at 18 goes with more attempts, but not with more deaths

Adjusted risk ratios (year, BMI, test centre, parents' education, IQ, height). For death alone, 0.96 is not significantly different from 1. Source: Åberg et al., Psychological Medicine, 2014 (online 2013).23,24

What this means

Young men with low fitness had about 79% more risk (× 1.79) of making an attempt or dying by suicide than those in good shape. But for deaths taken alone, no link appeared (× 0.96): the association comes from the attempts. The authors excluded men with a known psychiatric disorder, and the link held when comparing brothers, but they could not measure self-esteem or social situation. They conclude that it is not known whether improving fitness in adolescence reduces these behaviours.23

Two syntheses point the same way, with limits. A 2018 review finds less suicidal ideation in active than in inactive people (ratio of 0.87 across eight studies and 80,856 people), and more in those who do not meet the recommendations (1.16). The data are mostly cross-sectional, with poorly rigorous measures of activity.26 A 2024 review, focused on people with a mental disorder or a chronic illness, retained only seven studies (141,691 people): two case-control studies associate activity with fewer attempts, with no consistent link with suicidal ideation or with deaths, and without prospective data on attempts. The authors write that activity “could be linked to a lower frequency” of attempts.25

What this means

The three sources say the same thing, with different levels of evidence: physical activity is associated with less suicidal ideation and, perhaps, with fewer attempts. No source read establishes that exercise prevents deaths by suicide, or that a person who takes it up reduces their risk. It is sometimes said that people who die by suicide are “rarely in good physical shape”: no source read shows this, and the only large study of deaths by suicide does not find this link. The opposite reasoning also exists: depression reduces energy, so a person who is struggling may be less fit without low fitness being the cause.

Elite sport: performance sport is not health sport

An elite athlete does not automatically receive the protection described above. The International Olympic Committee consensus (2019) notes that symptoms of depression and anxiety there are broadly comparable to those of the general population, and that sport participation can be protective. But it lists risks specific to performance: serious injury, declining results, excessive perfectionism, overtraining.27 A review of 60 studies reaches the same idea of vulnerability, with a reservation: the quality of these studies is mostly limited.28

Overtraining illustrates this point. When the training load exceeds recovery, mood deteriorates, with depression being the component that rises most, and recovery can take weeks or even months.29 A 2025 review (16 studies, 692 athletes) associates higher volumes with more fatigue, tension and depressive symptoms; lightening the load improved emotional state.30

What this means

Dose matters in both directions. Moderate, regular exercise is associated with a better mental state. Training that overwhelms recovery can do the opposite. This signal matches that of the American study (more than 90 minutes per session, more than three hours a day), but it is for overtraining that the link is best documented.

Part 4 · The answer

What can we really expect from exercise when mental health wavers?

What is solid. Active people report fewer days of poor mental health and less depression, across hundreds of thousands of people, with a curve that starts from half the recommended dose. Randomised trials show on average a reduction in symptoms of depression and anxiety. The adverse effects reported in the trials are uncommon, mostly muscle or joint pain.11

What is probable. The effect is moderate, not miraculous: it shrinks with the most rigorous trials and its size remains uncertain. It appears comparable, in small trials, to psychotherapy or to a medication. All the forms tested have an effect, with no clear winner: the form you stick with matters more than the “optimal” form.

What is plausible but unproven. Improved sleep as a bridge between exercise and mood; the role of the brain (BDNF, inflammation); the role of social bond. Each has some clues, none is established as an explanation.

What has not been shown. That exercise prevents suicides. The data show a link with suicidal ideation, a possible link with attempts, and nothing clear with deaths. The frank answer is: we do not know. Exercise is a useful support for mental health, not a demonstrated prevention.

Where it reverses. When the training load exceeds recovery, mood deteriorates. When you are struggling, the first step remains to talk to someone.

Resources and help

3114

The national suicide prevention number: free, confidential, available 24 hours out of 24 and 7 days out of 7. It is intended for anyone who has suicidal thoughts and for their relatives. A trained nurse or psychologist answers.32

In case of immediate danger, call 15 (SAMU) or 112.32 If you are worried about someone, you can also call the 3114 to find out how to help them.

For sadness, anxiety or lack of motivation that lasts without suicidal thoughts, talk to your GP or a psychologist. Exercise adds to a treatment, it does not replace it, and asking for help is not a failure.

Part 5 · Putting it into practice

In practice: where to start, how much, how to track

These guidelines come from the data above; a simple piece of common-sense advice is flagged as such.

  1. Start at half the dose.About 75 minutes of moderate effort per week, spread over three or more sessions, already gives an associated benefit in the dose study.8 It is a realistic starting point, including if you are returning to exercise or struggling.
  2. Work up towards the official guidelines.The WHO recommends 150 to 300 minutes of moderate effort per week, and strength training on at least two days, stating that “some is better than none”.31 The American study associates the best mental state with three to five sessions of 30 to 60 minutes: this is only an association, use it as a reference point, not as a target to reach.7
  3. Choose what you will really do.Brisk walking, running, cycling, team sport, strength training, yoga: all the forms tested have an effect.13 If isolation weighs on you, exercise with others.
  4. Keep a recovery day and monitor your sleep.Sleep that deteriorates, fatigue that sets in and mood that drops while you are training more are signs of excess (common-sense advice, supported by the literature on overtraining).29,30 Ease off and ask for advice, rather than doing even more.
  5. See someone when it lasts.If sadness, anxiety or lack of motivation last several weeks, or interfere with your work or relationships, talk to a doctor or a mental health professional. Exercise adds to treatment, it does not replace it, and you do not stop a medication without medical advice.

What the THW test measures, and what it does not measure

The test on this page measures your physical fitness: a reference point for tracking the effect of your training, not a mental health test. The sources read do not allow a test score to be linked to a psychological state. Use it to see whether your practice is progressing, and repeat it under the same conditions, for example every 8 to 12 weeks (a practical rhythm, not one drawn from a study). For mood, a simple way to track how you are doing is to note your hours of sleep and your mood on a scale of 1 to 5 each week: this does not replace a validated questionnaire, but it gives you a trend to show your doctor if needed.

What these studies do not say
  • The effects are modest to moderate, measured on symptoms, not on a person's whole life.
  • Quality is uneven: 77 of the 97 reviews in the 2023 synthesis were rated “very low” quality with the AMSTAR-2 tool. The trials are often small.10
  • Publication bias: disappointing trials are published less often. Schuch (2016) concluded that it had not inflated the effect, but the risk remains.33
  • Part of the link between fitness and depression could be familial or genetic: in a Swedish study, the link decreases markedly when brothers are compared.34
  • The SMILE trial concerns adults aged 50 and over; the Swedish conscript study, men only. The results cannot be transposed as they are to everyone.14,23

Frequently asked questions

Can exercise replace a treatment?

No. The trials show that it helps, and that it appears comparable to a treatment in small trials, but this does not justify stopping a medication or a therapy without a doctor's advice.11

Does exercise protect against suicide?

This has not been shown. The data associate activity with less suicidal ideation and perhaps with fewer attempts, with no clear link to deaths. If you have suicidal thoughts, or if you are worried about someone, call the 3114.25,26,23

Can you do too much?

Yes. When training exceeds recovery, mood deteriorates, and the American study associates very large volumes with a poorer mental state.29,7
